title: Extreme Thrombocytosis in Patients With Malignancy; Complications, Management and Outcomes

paragraphs.en: Thrombocytosis is a frequently encountered haematological abnormality. However, extreme thrombocytosis (EXT), as defined by a platelet count of > 1000 × 109/L, is a rare entity. The aetiology of thrombocytosis can be classified as either primary (i.e., clonal thrombocytosis related to an underlying myeloproliferative neoplasm [MPN]) or secondary/reactive. There are limited data on the aetiology of EXT [1]. Historically, the majority of patients with EXT were assumed to have MPN. However, subsequent studies have demonstrated that as few as 10%–15% of cases of EXT are attributable to underlying MPN [2].

Malignancy is a known pro‐inflammatory state, but the exact pathophysiology of EXT in malignancy is complex and likely multifactorial, involving tumour‐mediated cytokine production (with IL‐6, IL‐1, and IL‐11 implicated), bone marrow stimulation and, in some cases, contributory processes such as infection or iron deficiency [2]. The clinical significance and prognostic implications of EXT in cancer patients remain unclear with little published evidence in this area. There are also limited data regarding the management of EXT in cancer patients. It is recognised that patients with EXT are at higher risk of both thrombotic and haemorrhagic complications [3]. For this reason, risk assessment is particularly important in this cohort as they have other risk factors for these complications (i.e., active malignancy, intercurrent infection and frequent admissions to hospital) [4].

We conducted a retrospective analysis of 220 patients with at least one documented occurrence of EXT at a dedicated cancer hospital (The Royal Marsden) over a 12‐year period (January 2010 to December 2022). We used a platelet count threshold of > 1000 × 109/L based on the widely used and accepted definition of EXT in the published literature. Patients were identified by an electronic search of laboratory records, and clinical data was collected regarding patient characteristics, underlying malignancy, investigations for thrombocytosis, thrombotic complications, management and outcomes. Patients with EXT who had either a new diagnosis of or prior history of MPN were excluded from analysis (n = 22).

One hundred and ninety‐eight patients were included in analysis. In terms of baseline characteristics, 113 patients were female (57%) and the median age at diagnosis of malignancy was 55 years (range 1–86). Most patients had non‐haematological malignancies (153, 77%). Of these, the most common diagnoses were lung cancer (39, 25%), pancreatic cancer (19, 12%) and bladder cancer (16, 10%). Haematological malignancy (non‐MPN) was the primary diagnosis in 45 patients (23%), the most common of which was Burkitt Lymphoma (12, 26%). Other cancer subtypes seen are outlined in Table 1.

The median highest platelet count reported in this patient population was 1112 × 109/L (range 1001–2593). MPN screening (JAK2, MPL, CALR and BCR‐ABL testing) was not done in the vast majority of patients; only 11 patients (5.5%) were tested.

Resolution of thrombocytosis, as defined by return to normal platelet count within one month of identification of EXT, was seen in 140 patients (71%), with the majority improving spontaneously (93, 66.5%). In 40 patients (28.5%), thrombocytosis improved with treatment of the underlying malignancy without requiring specific intervention, and in 5% it improved after treatment of intercurrent infection. Fifty‐six patients (28%) had persistent thrombocytosis, and resolution information was not available for two patients (1%).

In this patient population, 42 patients (21%) had a diagnosed thrombotic event during the study period. The majority of thromboses (35, 83%) were venous; pulmonary embolism (PE) was the most common thrombotic event and was seen in 13 patients (31% of those with thrombosis). Deep vein thrombosis (DVT) was diagnosed in 11 patients (26%). Seven patients (16%) had venous thrombosis at unusual sites, including renal vein, intra‐abdominal veins and gonadal vein. Four patients had line‐associated thrombosis (10%). The majority of these patients received anticoagulation; two patients (5%) did not, although the reason for this was not documented.

Arterial thrombotic events included cerebrovascular accident (4 patients, 9%), myocardial infarction (2, 5%) and splenic artery thrombosis (1, 2%). All of these patients were managed with antiplatelet therapy. One patient had both arterial and venous thrombotic events (1%).

The temporal relationship between EXT and thrombosis demonstrated a symmetrical distribution, with approximately 50% of thrombotic events diagnosed before and 50% after the identification of EXT. One quarter of thrombotic events occurred within ±1 month of EXT, while half occurred within ±3 months. Of note, 25 patients (59.5%) had concurrent thrombocytosis (platelet count > 400 × 109/L) at the time of thrombosis, and of these, 17 had persistent EXT. In patients with underlying haematological malignancy, the rate of thrombosis was 9%, compared to those with solid malignancy where 25% had a thrombotic event.

Antiplatelet therapy was used as thromboprophylaxis in 11 patients (5.5%). A subset of patients (11, 5.5%) were already receiving antiplatelet therapy prior to developing EXT and this was continued in these patients. Only one patient (0.5%) was started on therapeutic anticoagulation due solely to thrombocytosis.

The median follow‐up in this study was 14 months from time of EXT (range 0–177). Almost two‐thirds of patients had died at the time of analysis (129, 65%). The most common cause of death was malignancy (85, 66%). Infection was the cause of death in seven patients (5.5%), and in 35 patients (27%) the cause of death was unknown. Only two patients (1.5%) had a documented thrombotic cause of death (both CVA in patients with lung cancer). The median follow up from identification of EXT was 72 months (range 0–177), and 13 patients were lost to follow up (6.5%). The median Overall Survival (OS) was 26 months (range 0–336) from cancer diagnosis and 14 months from EXT onset. Of note, the median OS from EXT onset was shorter (7.5 months) in patients who developed thrombosis compared to those without a thrombotic event (14.5 months).

Forty‐four patients under the age of 18 with EXT were identified. Median platelet count was 1147 × 109/L (range 1001–1781). An MPN screen was done in only one patient and was negative. In most cases the thrombocytosis resolved; only two patients had persistent thrombocytosis (4.5%). Four patients had venous thrombotic events (9%), and two of these had concurrent thrombocytosis. No paediatric patients received aspirin or anticoagulation as thromboprophylaxis.

This study aimed to evaluate the clinical characteristics, management and outcomes of patients with malignancy who develop EXT, an area in which there is currently limited published evidence. In this large single‐centre cohort, we observed a higher rate of thrombotic events than reported in both general EXT populations and in unselected cancer populations. Thrombosis occurred in 21% of patients, notably higher than reported rates of 4%–6% in general EXT populations and 5%–6% in patients with malignancy overall [5, 6, 7]. Only 59.5% had thrombocytosis at the time of the thrombotic event, suggesting that EXT may represent one component of a multifactorial thrombotic process, rather than a primary causal factor. It is also possible that EXT serves as a surrogate marker of more aggressive disease biology or systemic inflammation, both of which are known to contribute to thrombotic risk. Thrombosis was seen at higher rates in patients with solid organ malignancy, and patients with thrombosis had a shorter median OS of 7.5 months (from EXT onset), compared to patients without a thrombotic event (14.5 months).

Several biological mechanisms may explain the association between EXT and thrombosis observed in our cohort. Malignancy‐associated thrombocytosis is thought to arise through tumour‐driven inflammatory pathways, particularly increased production of cytokines such as IL‐6, IL‐1 and IL‐11, which stimulate thrombopoietin production and megakaryopoiesis [5]. These inflammatory mediators also promote endothelial activation and coagulation, contributing to a prothrombotic state. In addition, platelets may contribute to cancer‐associated thrombosis through the release of procoagulant factors and interactions with tumour cells, leukocytes and neutrophil extracellular traps [8, 9]. Therefore, EXT may not simply represent a bystander phenomenon but could contribute to clot formation within an already hypercoagulable state. Alternatively, EXT may act as a surrogate marker of aggressive tumour biology, increased tumour burden or systemic inflammation, factors that are independently associated with both thrombotic risk and poorer survival outcomes. These mechanisms may also help explain the higher rate of thrombosis observed in patients with solid organ malignancies compared with haematological cancers.

Thromboprophylaxis was rarely commenced specifically for EXT (12 patients, 6%). Given that there was a higher thrombosis rate than is reported in patients with malignancy in general, this data suggests that consideration should be given to thromboprophylaxis in cancer patients with EXT. Further studies are required to further investigate what is the optimum prophylaxis regimen and duration.

MPN screening was infrequently performed. While routine screening in all patients with EXT may not be warranted, particularly when thrombocytosis is transient and clearly associated with an underlying cause, persistent or unexplained EXT may justify further haematological evaluation. Distinguishing between reactive and clonal thrombocytosis in this population is clinically challenging, yet essential, as it may influence both therapeutic strategies and outcomes.

The most common underlying malignancy seen in this cohort was lung cancer (25%), and there was also a significant number of gastrointestinal malignancies seen. This is comparable to published literature which indicates an association between EXT and these tumour types [10, 11].

The prevalence of EXT in paediatric patients with malignancy is notable, however the clinical implications of this are not well defined in the literature. Published data suggests a low thrombosis rate in those with reactive thrombocytosis [12]. Thom et al. reported on a series of paediatric patients with EXT and no thrombotic events were noted, albeit this patient group were not specifically those with underlying malignancy. The generally accepted practice is that paediatric patients do not routinely receive thromboprophylaxis in the absence of other risk factors [13]. The incidence of thrombotic events in our paediatric cohort (9%) is significantly higher than that previously reported and should prompt further study in this group.

This study has some limitations that should be considered when interpreting the results. The retrospective nature of the study means that there are some potential biases that can have an impact, such as possible under‐reporting of events or inaccurate/incomplete medical records which may affect data quality. Also, due to the observational nature of this study, it lacks a control group (i.e., patients with cancer but without EXT) that our results could have been compared to, which impacts our ability to determine causal relationships between variables.

In conclusion, EXT in malignancy appears to be associated with a higher observed rate of thrombotic events than expected, although causality cannot be established. These findings highlight the need for further prospective studies to better characterise the relationship between EXT and thrombosis in cancer patients, and to determine whether specific management strategies, including thromboprophylaxis or targeted investigation for MPN, may improve clinical outcomes.
